QUOTES • Those are good burgers Shut the fuck up Donny • I still jerk off manually • I’m The Dude • Yeah, well you know, that’s just like, your opinion man • That rug really tied the room together • I can’t be worrying about that shit, life goes on man NOTES One of my good friends Ryan Garner and I are doing a monthly movie review. This month’s theme was comedy and this was his pick. I’ve known Ryan since I was 15. He was a pallbearer for Whitney. He was one of the first people I called about my parents. He’s always been there for me. A really good friend. It was his house that I went to when my mom kicked me out at 15 (for doing what every 15 year old does). REVIEW Seeing Walter pull the gun at the bowling alley was rough. All I think about is my parents pulling their guns when I see guns. And the ashes at the end was rough too. Whitney is buried in West Jordan across from Gardner village. My dad is in a keychain I keep in my gym, along with the rest of his ashes in the urn from the mortuary. It’s incredibly hard to put the souls you loved most in a casket or an urn. I’ll never forget seeing my dad’s death certificate “shot in head”. Death really fucks with one’s mind. Sometimes I want to do something cool with my dad’s ashes and other times I’m so fucking pissed at him that I just don’t care about it. One day I think I’ll spread what’s in the keychain over Whitney’s resting spot so they can be together. After my dad would get done with his 2nd shift he would go to her graveside at night. My dad loved Whitney more than any parent loves their kid. And he loved me too. He had the biggest heart. My mom is still at my grandparents and idgaf what happens to her ashes. I hated seeing Jeff Bridges play the dude when to me he’s Kevin Flynn from Tron, who I compare to my Dad. And also Professor Lupin play a weirdo when to me he’ll always be Lupin who I also compare to my dad. The mom from crazy stupid love plays a weirdo too. Just an odd movie. Not my sense of humor. Too much hem and haw, the dialogue is so awkward and not thought out. And although I like some stupid movies. At least it’s regular guys in funny situations. Not dumb asses in a bad situation. Review: The Big Lebowski (1998) Rating: 2 / 5 stars The Big Lebowski has attained an almost mythical cult status in cinema history, but revisiting this Coen brothers comedy left me feeling largely detached from the hype. While the film certainly has its intermittent comedic moments and memorable characters, the overall package falls short of a cohesive cinematic experience. The Good: Moments of Genuine Humor To give credit where it is due, the film is not devoid of laughs. Jeff Bridges as "The Dude" embodies a wonderfully laid-back, bathrobe-wearing persona, and his bewildered reactions to the escalating absurdity around him provide a few genuine chuckles. John Turturro’s brief appearance as Jesus Quintana is undeniably eccentric, and select visual gags—particularly the elaborate, avant-garde dream sequences—showcase the Coen brothers' distinct stylistic flair. The Flaws: A Disjointed Plot Where the film truly struggles is its narrative structure. A good neo-noir parody or detective story relies on a convoluted plot that ultimately clicks into place, or at least unravels with a sharp satirical punch. Here, the plot feels less like a clever labyrinth and more like a meandering mess. The labyrinthine kidnapping scheme involving Jackie Treehorn, nihilists, and a severed toe feels more exhausting than engaging, dragging the runtime down significantly between the few comedic highlights. Lost in Translation: The Satire The movie's greatest weakness for me was its tone and satire. It attempts to spoof the hardboiled noir genre popularized by writers like Raymond Chandler, but the satire often feels too inside-itself, leaving the audience more lost than understanding. Instead of a biting commentary on Los Angeles crime tropes or slackers, it frequently devolves into a series of bizarre, loosely connected vignettes that prioritize weirdness over substance or clarity. Final Verdict Ultimately, The Big Lebowski feels less like a masterclass in comedy and more like an over-indulgent time-capsule noir piece that relies too heavily on quirkiness to mask a weak narrative core. If you deeply vibe with its ultra-slack pacing and absurdist tangents, there is fun to be had; otherwise, it is a frustratingly elusive watch.

Diría que la comedia debe de ser el género más complicado dentro de la subjetividad cinematográfica. Una película cómica necesita provocar risas, al igual que una dramática necesita despertar la empatía oculta. ¿Qué pasa cuando una comedia no genera gracia al espectador? Bien, este ha sido mi caso con *El gran Lebowski*. La historia nos pone en los zapatos de Jeff Lebowski/Dude, un idiota perroflauta que se mete en una misión de millonarios. El contraste entre la solemnidad del Gran Lebowski y la de Dude es gracioso. El viejo es alguien elegante y bien hablado; en cambio, Dude es un porrero que va en bata o con ropa de estar por casa todo el día. La tarea que le dan a Jeff es sencilla: dar un millón de dólares a los secuestradores de Bunny. La esposa de Lebowski es una jovencita que está buena y que está con el anciano por dinero. Es decir, estamos ante una sugar baby que está con un carcamal. Que Lebowski esté con una niñata así demuestra su vanidad y su necesidad de mostrarle a la gente su poder económico mediante la compra de una joven actriz porno. Seguramente lo necesite porque no tiene nada realmente a su nombre y anhela ser poderoso. Todos esos discursos que le da a Jeff sobre el trabajo son pura mierda viniendo de él. «Con los ricos y poderosos siempre un poco de paciencia». Jeff hará su misión con Walter... Oh, Walter, ¡qué pesado me has parecido! Walter debe de ser uno de los personajes más insoportables que he visto en una película, en general. Pierde los nervios y, en vez de hablar, grita todo el rato gilipolleces. Hasta Jeff lo sabe, pero no dice nada por cariño. Entre que relaciona todo con Vietnam, se cree el Rambo de los bolos, apunta con armas al hispano pedófilo... Yo creo que Walter es un personaje que no despierta indiferencia: o te hace mucha gracia, o se te hace pesado. El otro gran compañero de bolos es Donny, quien no tiene un rol en la película. Solo se dedica a «interrumpir» debido a que no se entera de lo que hablan y quiere ser incluido. En general, su función es que Walter grite, nada más. Su muerte tiene un chiste que debería hacer gracia sobre dónde le han disparado, pero, como no le han disparado, simplemente sufre un infarto. Hablando de la protagonista femenina, Maude Lebowski, no me ha parecido súper graciosa. Juliane Moore me pareció muy graciosa en *Boogie Nights* o en *Kingsman*, por decir algo más moderno, pero en esta película me ha sabido a poco. Es la hija cínica del Gran Lebowski y su «relación» con Jeff es follar para quedarse embarazada. Ella odia a su padre por ser un inútil, como Jeff, pero que se las da de importante por haber heredado lo que su esposa tenía. No está mal para despertar risas, pero a mí no me ha llegado ese personaje. Si tú me das cinismo, tienes que hacerlo con un argumento que lo justifique. La misión se desarrolla con momentos cómicos y algunos momentos insoportables de Walter, como la escena de la cafetería. Luego descubrimos que no había millón de dólares y todo era una farsa para librarse de esa actriz porno de poca monta. Los «villanos» alemanes son bastante idiotas. Me hace gracia que su característica sea el nihilismo y estén desmotivados durante todas sus acciones. No está mal, pero cuando veo ese duelo final con la bola de bolos y a Walter arrancando una oreja... apagué el cerebro. Cuando al final sale el narrador, pensé que esto era una broma. Es un cowboy cualquiera que es la voz narrativa y dice: «Al final, Dude está tranquilo por todos nosotros». Gracias, Dios de los vaqueros, no pensé que el porreta iba a estar tranquilo después de esto. Hablando de la fotografía y la cinematografía, he de decir que me han gustado. Aunque sea de película de serie B, he de decir que me gusta que sea intencional. La historia es cómica y no necesitas una fotografía IMAX 70 mm. La banda sonora es una delicia. Los Coen tienen un gusto muy bueno para las canciones. Ya sea cuando Dude escucha su mixtape o cuando está alucinando, sabes que hay un temazo de fondo. Las escenas alucinativas están bien, pero tampoco me han pillado con las ganas de encontrármelas. Son escenas que vemos mientras Jeff está inconsciente y sirven para ver cómo su mente interpreta los acontecimientos que vive. La actuación de Jeff Bridges es la mejor, la verdad. Me sorprende que la película haya reunido a Bridges, Philip Seymour Hoffman y Juliane Moore. Las actuaciones, muy bien. A modo de conclusión, quiero decir que la película tiene la base y todo lo necesario para ser graciosa y que a una vasta mayoría le encante, pero a mí precisamente no me ha pillado gracioso. Creo haber destacado todos los demás aspectos de forma positiva (actuaciones, fotografía, banda sonora y, en cierto modo, la historia), pero su comedia no me ha encandilado. Entonces volvemos a la premisa: ¿una película cómica puede ser buena si no puede hacerte reír? Mi respuesta es sí, pero si el resto de cosas consiguen compensar esa carencia. Si la película depende íntegramente de la comedia y a alguien, por alguna razón, no le ha hecho gracia, no pasa nada; tal vez le haga gracia otro día o nunca se la genere.

So this is the movie everyone fucking loves? Was The Big Lebowski funny? Yes. Was it the funniest movie I've ever seen? Yeah... NO. I went into this with pretty high expectations because I've heard so many people call this one of the funniest movies ever made. I also really like the Coen brothers, so I was expecting to laugh my ass off. I didn't. Not once. And that's probably the biggest problem I had with it. I understood the jokes, I thought the characters were funny, and I could see why people love it, but I just never found myself actually laughing out loud. It was more like sitting there thinking, “Okay, that's pretty funny.” The story itself worked really well though. It's such a stupid fucking situation that somehow keeps getting more complicated. The Dude gets mistaken for someone else, gets dragged into this whole kidnapping situation and suddenly he's involved in all kinds of bullshit he clearly doesn't want to be involved in. And then there's Walter. Walter is probably my favorite part of the movie. This man is fucking insane. Every single situation somehow turns into a war because Walter refuses to just chill for five seconds. And the gag with Donny constantly trying to talk while Walter tells him to shut up every time was pretty funny. Poor Donny just wanted to participate. I also have to talk about Peter Stormare because I fucking love that dude. He barely has anything to do in this movie compared to some of the other characters, but he was still great. Every time he showed up I was like, “YOOOO IT'S PETER STORMARE.” His character is basically just this weird, silent, intimidating Swedish guy who looks like he's about to commit a crime at any second. I don't even know what it is about him, but I just love watching this man in movies. The characters were definitely the strongest part of the movie. The Dude is obviously iconic. He's basically a man who has completely given up on life and somehow still gets dragged into every possible problem. He doesn't even seem surprised anymore when something ridiculous happens. Walter is the complete opposite. He treats every tiny problem like it's a military operation. And Donny is just... there. I also really liked how bowling was basically connected to everything. I didn't expect the movie to lean this hard into bowling, but somehow it worked. You have this ridiculous crime story happening, but everyone is still somehow finding time to go bowling. That was probably the most unique thing about the movie for me. Because honestly, I didn't find much else that stood out. The cinematography was fine, but nothing really blew me away. It looked like a normal movie to me. There weren't many shots where I thought, “Holy shit, that looks amazing.” And that's usually something I really appreciate in movies. I also think I expected the whole thing to feel more unique. Everyone talks about The Big Lebowski like it's this completely insane experience that you've never seen anything like before. And while the characters definitely have their own personalities, the actual movie didn't feel THAT special to me. Maybe that's why I didn't connect with it as much as I wanted to. I know this is one of those movies that has a massive fanbase and I can absolutely understand why. It's well written, the characters are memorable, the dialogue works, and the whole story is pretty damn entertaining. I just wasn't laughing. And when your entire reputation is being one of the funniest movies ever, that's kind of a problem for me. I still had a good time watching it though. It was never boring and I definitely don't regret watching it. I just expected something way more memorable, especially after hearing people hype this movie up for years. Maybe I'll appreciate it more on a rewatch. Maybe I was just in the wrong mood. Maybe I need to become a professional bowler first. For now though, it's just a good movie to me. 6/10 bowling balls TIM OUT Good watch, but bro... where was the fucking laughter?

The Big Lebowski is one of those films that is unapologetically different; quirky and absurd, meandering and carefree, hilarious and ‘slap in the face’ crude at times. It is a film that seems to be ridiculous for the sake of it, but looking a bit deeper, it is almost a conceptual adaptation of the film The Big Sleep and many other old noirs, and it hides an ingenious commentary on a century old film law that will change the way you see it forever. The film is very entertaining throughout the entire two hour showing, and features the classic unique humor of films common before the marvel era. The editing often adds to the hilarity of many moments, –particularly when ‘the Dude’ as Lebowski likes to call himself is drugged or unconscious–but it is low-key for most of the film to match the mood. The film also feels very real, as the Mise-en-sćene is on point, capturing the Dude’s lazy lifestyle in the grubbiness of his house and the favorite bathrobe which he always wears. The music is similarly on point, and the needledrops somehow set the correct mood just about every time. The dialogue is quirky and a little weird sometimes, which admittedly matches the overall vibe of the film, as do the abundant F-bombs permeating the entirety of the show. The story however is the biggest ‘strength’ of the movie if I may be so bold as to call it that. Borrowing from many common tropes of classic noir and mystery films, The Big Lebowski takes them and twists them ingeniously with the anti-hero archetype, to write a story about a deadbeat loser who likes bowling being thrown into a mystery with his life at stake. It is presented well for the most part, and though I'm not a fan of how some of the storytelling is omniscient, the laidback and unhurried feel of the story make up for it. At the very start of the movie, the narrator, when talking about the Dude says “I won’t call him a Hero–Because what is a hero?–but sometimes there’s a man…the man for his time and place” and the rest of the movie struggles with this question, and Dude’s identity as an unlikely hero, ultimately exploring the themes of impermanence, how to abide in an indifferent world, and the virtue of enjoying a simple life. (Bonus: The Hays Code/Adaptation Theory) There is another way to look at The Big Lebowski, which re-contextualizes everything about the way we see it. In adaptation theory, there are three main types of adaptations, Literal, Traditional, and Radical/Analogical. This new way to look at The Big Lebowski sees the film as a radical adaptation of The Big Sleep, a noir film we previously watched. We can see parallels between the two films left and right, but there’s one major difference, the Hays code. The Hays code was a rule in filmmaking implemented in the 1930’s that prohibited the inclusion of any immoral or violent content into the films. The Big Lebowski seems to be a commentary on the Hays code; a loose adaptation of The Big Sleep but without skirting around all the questionable content. For some people this is a massive revelation and changes their entire perspective of the film, and while I love the creative and innovative idea, my perspective on the movie wasn’t drastically altered because of this particular, seemingly random reference. Overall, The Big Lebowski is a good Noir-Parody/Comedy film that loves a good laugh and an F-bomb, with a likable antihero and an interesting story behind its adaptation.

The Dude abides. He doesn’t align with an ideology, he doesn’t classify himself as anything but The Dude. He isn’t deeply opinionated or bound by his roots and his past. He simply does what makes him happy and content. He goes bowling, he smokes weed and most importantly he has his rug which really ties the room together. Throughout the film he is constantly dragged away from his simple life by people of all types of ideologies. The nihilists, the fascists, war veterans, corrupt pornographers and of course the big Lebowski. What connects all these different factions is LA; early 90s LA. The specific time and location where all of these people of strong beliefs congest and complicate life for the dude. He’s simply a tumbleweed in the wind, dragged literally and figuratively into the web of crime and corruption often by Walter. Walter who is constantly exploding into violence yet claims he once dabbled in pacifism. The Coens create such an amusing critique of ideologies using the contrast to the dude. Every other character is driven by money, sex or violence despite what they say. Even Maude and Donny aren’t as pure as the dude as they both seek out sex/money by the end, despite generally being very good characters. The Coens show how nobody truly follows their beliefs and every character contradicts themselves. The Nihilists don’t care about anything yet constantly pursue the ransom money. The big lebowski acts like a successful man yet it’s all a facade to get money in the first place. Then the film takes a turn towards the end as it carries through the character development and commentary from the first half and starts to become an outlook on the human condition. “I guess that's the way the whole durned human comedy keeps perpetuatin' itself down through the generations. Westward the wagons, across the sands of time” . That’s what this film is at its core, a human comedy. Balancing nihilism and cynicism whilst being the funniest and most quotable film of all time.
